input.instructions: Create a compact, accurate blueprint for an 8-to-12-minute educational lesson with exactly ten sequential teaching beats. Do not write full narration. Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.

Topic: CSCI-603: Computational Problem Solving. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course focuses on the application of computational thinking using a problem-centered approach. Specific topics include: expression of algorithms in pseudo-code and a programming language; elementary data structures such as lists, trees and graphs; problem solving using recursion; and debugging and testing. Assignments (both in class and homework) requiring a pseudo-code solution and implementation in a programming language are an integral part of the course. Note: This course serves as a bridge course for graduate students and cannot be taken by undergraduate students without permission from the CS Undergraduate Program Coordinator. This course is restricted to students in COMPSCI-MS. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring Every beat must be directly relevant to that catalog description. Prefer the RIT catalog source for scope claims. Use a supplemental source only when its cited claim teaches a named course topic; never use an unrelated source merely to fill a claim slot. Keep production directions exclusively in visualDirection and never say phrases such as 'on screen', 'show on screen', 'cut to', or 'camera' in narration. Regeneration revision 4: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[opendsa-programming-foundations]
Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax. Variables represent values and state, expressions compute values, and control structures select or repeat operations. Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results. Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case. Lists represent ordered sequences, stacks use last-in first-out access, queues use first-in first-out access, trees represent hierarchy, and graphs represent connected entities. Searching and sorting algorithms depend on representation and invariants. Correctness arguments, tests, tracing, and debugging compare intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.

[python-language-reference]
The Python language reference specifies lexical analysis, data model behavior, execution, expressions, statements, functions, classes, exceptions, and module import semantics. Python objects have identity, a type, and a value. Names are bound to objects within namespaces and scopes. Expressions produce values, while statements control execution and bindings. Exceptions interrupt normal control flow until a matching handler processes them or they propagate. The import system searches for modules and binds loaded modules into a namespace. Programs should be reasoned about through explicit state, control flow, data representation, contracts, tests, and observable behavior. Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while decomposition and abstraction reduce the number of interacting concerns.

beats.claim: Programming begins with precise problem statements, input and output examples, and algorithms written independently of syntax.
beats.example: A student must write a function that takes a list of integers and returns the sum of all even numbers, clearly defining the input format and expected output before writing any code.
beats.title: Defining the Computational Problem
beats.visualDirection: Display a structured template with labeled sections for 'Problem Statement', 'Input Specification', 'Output Specification', and 'Constraints' to guide the learner in drafting their own problem definition.

beats.claim: Functions decompose a solution into named operations with parameters and results, allowing complex tasks to be broken into manageable units.
beats.example: To calculate the average of a dataset, one function reads the input, a second function filters out non-numeric values, and a third computes the mean, each with clear parameters and return values.
beats.title: Decomposing with Functions
beats.visualDirection: Show a flowchart where a large 'Compute Average' block branches into three smaller, labeled blocks: 'Read Input', 'Filter Data', and 'Calculate Mean', illustrating functional decomposition.

beats.claim: Recursion solves a problem through smaller instances and requires a base case to terminate the process.
beats.example: Calculating the factorial of 5 involves calling the function with 4, then 3, down to 1 (the base case), where the result is returned without further recursive calls.
beats.title: Understanding Recursion
beats.visualDirection: Render a tree diagram where the root node is 'Factorial(5)' and each child node represents a recursive call (e.g., 'Factorial(4)'), terminating at leaf nodes labeled 'Base Case: n=1'.

beats.claim: Lists represent ordered sequences, providing a fundamental way to store and access collections of items in a specific order.
beats.example: A student's grade list [85, 90, 78, 92] allows sequential access to each score and supports operations like appending a new grade or removing the lowest one.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Lists
beats.visualDirection: Present a horizontal array graphic with numbered indices above each element, highlighting the ordered nature of the list and demonstrating an 'append' action adding a new value at the end.

beats.claim: Trees represent hierarchy, organizing data in parent-child relationships that naturally model nested or branching structures.
beats.example: A file system directory structure is a tree where the root is the main drive, branches are folders, and leaves are individual files, enabling efficient traversal and organization.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Trees
beats.visualDirection: Draw a binary tree with a root node labeled 'Root', two child nodes labeled 'Left' and 'Right', and further descendants to visually demonstrate hierarchical nesting.

beats.claim: Graphs represent connected entities, modeling relationships between objects where nodes are entities and edges denote connections.
beats.example: A social network graph connects users as nodes and friendships as edges, allowing algorithms to find the shortest path between two people or identify communities.
beats.title: Elementary Data Structures: Graphs
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a network of circles (nodes) linked by lines (edges), with one node highlighted to show its connections, emphasizing the relational aspect of graphs.

beats.claim: Correctness arguments rely on invariants—conditions that remain true throughout an algorithm's execution—to prove that the solution meets its specification.
beats.example: In a sorting algorithm, the invariant 'the subarray to the left of the current index is sorted' holds true after each iteration, guaranteeing the final array is fully sorted.
beats.title: Algorithmic Invariants and Correctness
beats.visualDirection: Show a timeline of a loop with a highlighted invariant statement persisting across iterations, visually reinforcing that the condition is maintained throughout the process.

beats.claim: Debugging separates syntax, runtime, and logical failures, while testing compares intended behavior with observable results, including boundary and error cases.
beats.example: A tester runs a function with an empty list (boundary case) and a list containing only negative numbers (error case) to verify the program handles these scenarios without crashing.
beats.title: Debugging and Testing Strategies
beats.visualDirection: Display a split-screen view: one side shows a code snippet with a syntax error highlighted, the other shows a test case output indicating a logical failure, illustrating the debugging workflow.

beats.claim: Assignments require expressing algorithms first in pseudo-code to clarify logic before translating into a specific programming language like Python.
beats.example: A student writes a step-by-step pseudo-code description of a binary search algorithm, then converts each step into Python syntax, ensuring the logic remains unchanged.
beats.title: Pseudo-code to Implementation
beats.visualDirection: Present a side-by-side comparison: the left column contains high-level pseudo-code steps, and the right column shows the corresponding Python code lines, with arrows linking matching operations.

beats.claim: Before finalizing any solution, verify that the problem statement is precise, the chosen data structures match the requirements, recursion has a clear base case, and tests cover in
beats.example: A checklist item asks: 'Does the algorithm handle the edge case where the input list is empty?' followed by 'Are all recursive calls reducing the problem size?'
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Render a compact checklist graphic with four tick-box items: 'Precise Problem Statement', 'Appropriate Data Structures', 'Valid Recursive Base Case', and 'Comprehensive Test Coverage', each with a brief prompt.
